summary: This standards-track RFC defines an EDNS(0) Padding option so DNS clients and servers can pad requests and responses by a variable number of octets. Padding makes message sizes less revealing when DNS traffic is encrypted.

plainLanguage.summary: Putting a letter in a bigger envelope with filler so nobody can guess what it says from its size.

questions: dns padding to hide message size
can i use dns padding without encryption
subtitle: A DNS option that lets clients and servers add filler bytes so encrypted messages reveal less through their size.

tldr.problem: Even when DNS messages are encrypted, their size is metadata that can be used to correlate them with well-known unencrypted messages.
tldr.mechanism: The EDNS(0) Padding option (option code 12) lets a client or server add a variable number of padding octets inside the OPT record, which hides the true size of the message.
tldr.outcome: Padding only helps on encrypted transport, so implementations MUST NOT use the option when the DNS transport is not encrypted.

facts.label: Occurrences
facts.value: At most once per OPT meta-RR

today: RFC 7830 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. IANA updated the registry record for option code 12 to reference this RFC with status Standard.

sections.title: Why Pad Encrypted DNS
sections.content:
DNS was specified to carry messages in cleartext, which can expose a lot about an end user's Internet activity. The IETF has worked on confidentiality for DNS transactions, and encrypting the transport is one option.

RFC 7830 points out that even if queries and responses were both encrypted, metadata could still be used to correlate them with well-known unencrypted messages. One such property is message size. The RFC defines the EDNS(0) Padding option so that clients and servers can artificially increase a DNS message by a variable number of bytes, which hampers size-based correlation.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a sealed letter shows how big it is. Adding filler makes every letter look about the same size.

sections.title: The Padding Option
sections.content:
EDNS(0) (RFC 6891) lets new options ride in the RDATA of the OPT meta-RR. The Padding option consists of an OPTION-CODE of 12, an OPTION-LENGTH that is the size in octets of the padding, and then the padding octets. The minimum number of padding octets is 0. The option MUST occur at most once per OPT meta-RR, and therefore at most once per message.

The padding octets SHOULD be set to 0x00. Other values MAY be used, for example when there is concern that the padded message could be compressed before encryption. Receivers MUST accept padding octets of any value.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small label saying 'filler here' and how much of it there is. The filler is usually just blank space.

sections.title: When to Pad
sections.content:
The RFC does not say how much to pad, because that depends on the situation. A padded message MUST NOT exceed the number of octets in the Requestor's Payload Size field, which is encoded in the RR Class field.

  • Responders MUST pad a response when the query included the Padding option, unless that would violate the maximum UDP payload size.
  • Responders MAY pad a response when the query showed EDNS(0) support but did not include the option.
  • Responders MUST NOT pad a response when the query did not indicate EDNS(0) support.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for a padded answer you get one, if you only seem able to handle it you might get one, and if you cannot handle it you never do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Padding makes packets bigger, so it leads to more traffic. It gives a benefit only when DNS packets are not sent in cleartext, and it may make DNS amplification attacks easier. Therefore implementations MUST NOT use the option if the DNS transport is not encrypted.

Padding length might be changed by lower-level compression, so implementations and deployments SHOULD disable compression at the Transport Layer Security (TLS) level, as described in Section 3.3 of RFC 7525. The RFC also notes that the padding payload could be used as a covert channel, like many other fields in DNS. IANA has assigned Option Code 12 for Padding.
sections.plainLanguage: Filler only helps if the letter is sealed, it makes the mail heavier, and someone could hide a secret note in the filler.
